---
title: "xvrt"
subtitle: "GDAL multidimensional VRT from xarray Datasets and STAC catalogues"
---

xvrt writes [GDAL multidimensional VRT](https://gdal.org/en/stable/drivers/raster/vrt_multidimensional.html)
files: small XML documents that describe a collection of files as one
n-dimensional dataset. The VRT holds no data. It records which file supplies
which slab of which array, plus the dimensions, coordinates, CRS, units and
packing, so any reader of GDAL's multidimensional API opens the whole
collection as a single cube and reads only the files a request touches.

It is pure Python (no GDAL needed to write) and has two front doors:

- **From xarray.** Open a set of files the way you normally would, then
  describe the result with `write_mdim_vrt(ds, sources, path)`. The Dataset's
  dims, coordinates, attributes and encoding say what the cube looks like; the
  source list says where its pieces live.
- **From a STAC catalogue.** `from_stac(items, path)` builds the VRT from
  catalogue fields alone (grid, CRS, datetimes, band storage), without opening
  a single file.

::: {#8753181b .cell execution_count=1}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
xvrt 0.1.0
```
:::
:::


## A recipe, not a payload

Opening a long time series of files is expensive work: coordinates are read,
dimensions aligned, packing and time decoded. Most tools do this work each
time and then throw the result away. A VRT keeps it as a portable text
artifact that GDAL, and anything built on GDAL, can reuse directly. It sits
between the file collection and the analysis: no bytes are copied, and the
description can be versioned, shared and inspected like any other text file.

## Install

```bash
pip install xvrt
pip install "xvrt[stac]"   # adds pyarrow and pyproj for from_stac()
```

Requirements are `numpy` and `xarray`. Reading stac-geoparquet needs
`pyarrow`; turning an EPSG code into WKT needs `pyproj` (or GDAL's Python
bindings). Reading the result needs GDAL 3.x with multidimensional support.
